title: Katharina von Bora
hook: a nun who escaped, tradition says, in a herring cart, married Luther, and ran a brewery, farm and household

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Wartburg: Luther in hiding as Knight George, translating for the market. Your line was the language of the market.

Behind a convent wall, in the days before Easter, a group of nuns have been reading pamphlets smuggled in from Wittenberg, and they've decided to leave. Leaving is dangerous. A merchant who brings goods to the convent agrees to help. One night his covered cart rolls away loaded with empty barrels, barrels that once held herring, tradition says. Tucked among them, hardly breathing, are the nuns. The cart makes it out. Among the women who climb down at the other end, smelling of fish, is Katharina von Bora.

Katharina had been placed in a convent as a girl. Now she was out, with no money and no family able to take her in, and the reformers tried to find husbands for the women who had left. For Katharina, a match was tried and fell through. Then, the story goes, she let it be known she would marry Luther, or one other man, and no one else. Luther was surprised, and then he did it. They moved into his old monastery building in Wittenberg, and she turned it into a household. She brewed beer. She kept a farm, cows and pigs, a garden, an orchard and a fishpond. She fed students who boarded with them, and refugees, and a stream of guests who came to argue theology at her table. She managed the money, which was not Luther's gift. She nursed the sick, and she raised their children. Luther's letters to her are full of teasing affection. He calls her my lord Katie, putting the word for a lord or master in front of her name. He calls her a rich woman, a doctor, a preacher, a brewer. In his will he left everything to her, which surprised people at the time. Proverbs has a poem for a woman like this, the capable wife. In the King James Bible: "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." Catholic and Lutheran readers tell her story differently. For Catholics, leaving a convent broke solemn vows. For the reformers, marriage was a holy calling too. Either way, a movement runs on someone who keeps the house standing.

Bring to mind one person whose work keeps your life running and mostly goes unseen: someone who cooks, schedules, cleans, remembers birthdays, pays the bills. Think of one specific thing they did this week. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold that one thing with gratitude.
Katharina. The nun who escaped in a wagon of barrels, married Luther, and ran the brewery, farm and household at the heart of the Wittenberg reform.
Your line: my lord katie. Luther's teasing names were love in plain words. Day eight hundred fifty-six, complete.

howItsDone: Lutheran churches remember Katharina von Bora, and some honor her in their calendars of commemoration; her household is often held up in Protestant teaching as a picture of the pastor's family and home.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, ages or counts stated (the number of nuns, her age, the number of children are left out). The herring detail is attributed to tradition; the hook field is reworded to say so. 'Night, before Easter' (Easter Eve 1523) and the merchant Leonhard Koppe are general history; confirm.
'She would marry Luther, or one other man' (Nikolaus von Amsdorf) is framed as 'the story goes'; confirm.

Household details (brewing, farm, livestock, fishpond, boarders, guests, nursing, managing money) are general history from biographies, not from the cited letters; confirm. 'Which Luther was terrible at' is informal; confirm tone.
Luther's names for her in letters ('Herr Käthe', 'my lord Katie', also 'Doctor', 'preacher', 'brewer', 'rich woman of Zülsdorf') paraphrased; confirm each.
Luther's will leaving everything to her (contrary to the custom of the time) is general history; confirm.
Fairness: Catholic view (broken vows) and reformers' view (marriage as a holy calling) given side by side without ranking. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'by his account' cut from the hook (no account by the merchant is cited); invented portrait detail ('a firm chin') cut; 'several matches fell through' (a count) changed to a single failed match (Baumgärtner), confirm; 'which Luther was terrible at' softened; closing contrast names Catholic and Lutheran readers instead of a generic 'Christians see her story differently'.
Original: 'Herr Käthe' — confirm spelling and that it is used in Luther's letters.

Second editor: hook no longer opens on a wagon (day 855 opened on a wagon on a forest road); it now starts behind the convent wall with the pamphlets, and the merchant (Koppe, who supplied the convent) is described without a name; 'young' cut.
Auditor (day 847-856 pass): checked; Proverbs 31:27 matches the KJV; Luther's names for her (Herr Käthe, doctor, preacher, brewer) and the household details are standard history. No change.
